tei:titleStmt.tei:title: יום טוב של ק״ק קאוואליאון לכ״ט בחדש סיון
Poetic Additions for 29 Sivan, a barely-avoided blood-libel pogrom in Cavaillon (1713)

tei:div.tei:head: Poetic Additions for 29 Sivan, a barely-avoided blood-libel pogrom in Cavaillon (1713)

tei:l.tei:note: Verses recited before the festival night
of the holy community of Cavallion on 29 Sivan,
and the included v-Al haNisim piyyut,
composed by the great and noble poet, rabbi and teacher,
Rabbi Gad son of Rabbi Yehudah de Bédarride

tei:lg.tei:l: I thank the Cause wholeheartedly,
in the upright council and assembly. (Psalms 111:1)
Making great wonders alone,
for eternal is Their kindness! (Psalms 136:4)
And saved us from our stressors,
for eternal is Their kindness (Psalms 136:24)
I will exalt the Cause for I was low,
but my enemies did not rejoice over me. (Psalms 30:2)
You turned my mourning into a dance for me,
opened my sackcloth and girded me with joy (Psalms 30:12)
In congregations, bless God,
the Master, from the source of Israel. (Psalms 68:27)
Bless God in congregations!
In congregations sing, yearning assembly,
and trust in the Cause;
And in my myriad assembly, in congregations,
bless God the Cause.
O Cause, save!
May the Sovereign answer us on the day we call. (Psalms 20:10)

tei:l.tei:note: And finish the evening prayer as a regular weekday,
and when reading “Forever we have hoped in You” say:

tei:lg.tei:l: For the miracles
and for the rescue
and for the mighty acts
that You repaid and did for us
and our children and for our descendants
On the twenty-ninth day of the month of Sivan
in the year 5473,
an assembly of the corrupt and evil rose against us —
worthless are they, a work of delusions! (Jeremiah 10:15)
Regarding what they found on their iniquitous day:
a lad, killed, lacking blood.
It almost became a stumbling-block for us,
as they said “We seek his blood from your hands!”
And these wicked ones gathered against us,
schemed secretly,
and sought to destroy to the very foundation.
For they said “Let’s go annihilate them from nationhood,
that the name of Israel not be remembered;” (Psalms 83:5)
scheme your schemes, and they will be overturned,
say your piece, and it will not come about,
for the Deity is with us! (Isaiah 8:10)
And they came against us with libel,
into our courtyards by the track,
in darkest night and gloom (Proverbs 7:9)
In the night, sleep fled the Sovereign;
the highest ones fled to seek rescue
for the poor and wandering people.
Not in our merit,
only in the merit of the mighty ones,
and the merit of those nursing from breasts and little ones.
They searched and inquired and sought
in all our houses
to see if they could find a drop of blood,
or even a reddish stain.
And the good Shepherd saved us
from the mouth of lions and bears,
for if they had found anything they could rely on
they would have made destruction upon the enemies of Israel,
for the mob’s voice already came out:
“The Jews killed him with a strong hand!”
We went through fire and water,
and You brought us out to relief.
As they would say it is our custom each and every year,
killing a young lad callously,
as a proverb and byword —
and this is nothing but a pretext.
Avenge our vengeance, Dweller on High,
for the dove has not found rest!
And for this we established this stressful day
as a day of joy and cheer;
our lips exalting songs and laudations,
praise and hymn without pleas,
only a holiday to thank and praise and laud and glorify
for the miracle that You did to the people small in faith.
And You were for us a shield and buckler,
and thus we established upon us
and those who come after us each and every year.
Let she who is chained rejoice,
and give a herald to Jerusalem!
And we will thank Your great name,
selah.

tei:l.tei:note: Before taking out the Torah: Psalms 55

tei:lg.tei:l: To the conductor, arioso,
a lesson of David.
Listen, God, to my prayer;
and do not hide from my plea.
Hearken to me and answer me,
I am restless in my murmering and moaning
at the enemy’s sound, from the wicked’s oppression,
for they drop evil upon me, in rage oppose me.
My heart trembles inside me,
and death’s terrors fall upon me.
Fear and trembling come upon me,
I am covered in horror.
And I said, “Who would give me wings like a dove,
so I could fly off and shelter!?
Surely I would flee far,
I would dwell in the wilds — selah —
I would hurry to a refuge for me,
from the sweeping storming wind.”
Swallow up, divide their speech, Cause;
for I see violence and strife in the city!
Day and night they surround its walls,
evil and toil are within it.
Ruin is within it,
fraud and deceit never leave its plaza.
As it is not an enemy that curses me —
that, I could bear —
nor those who hate me powerful against me —
I could hide from them —
It is you, a man like me, my known companion!
We would sweetly counsel!
In the house of God we would walk in the throng!
Let death be lent upon them!
Let them go down to the underworld alive,
for evil is where they dwell, among them.
And I to God will call,
to the Cause who will save me.
Evening and morning and noon, I would murmer and moan,
and They heard my voice.
They redeemed my soul from my battle,
for many were with me.
The Deity, dwelling of old — selah — who has no successor, hears and humbles
those not reverent of God.
He sent his hand against his ally,
profaned his treaty;
smoother than butter his mouth,
while his mind was on war;
softer than oil his words,
but they were curse-swords.
Cast your burden on the Cause who will sustain you;
They will not let the righteous man ever falter.
And You, God, will bring them down to the lowest pit;
these bloody deceitful people will not live half their days,
but I will trust in You.

tei:l.tei:note: And take out the Torah scroll
and three people read from Parashat B’shallaḥ
the Song written for the festival day of the holy community of Carpentras.

tei:note.tei:p: In the Modim prayer, the final passage before an Al haNissim addition is inserted.
Find Esther 6:1. The angels begged God to save Israel from destruction.
A common poetic term for the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob

The root ḥpś is usually found in the pi’el, but here is found in the pa’al. This is not a typo, merely a poetic form. See Proverbs 2:4 and Proverbs 20:27, Psalms 64:7, and Lamentations 3:40 for other instances of it.
While often associated with Christianity, this term is also found in the midrashic literature for God.
The followng line in the Modim prayer.
In a rare psalmodic turn, the text directly rebukes the enemy. With the context of a blood libel, this could perhaps be read as a mournful recollection of Christianity’s Jewish origin.
The ketiv here is ישימות, giving “Desolation be upon them!”
Some commentators read this word, literally “opened ones,” as “swords,” others as “curses.” I’ve included both to be safe.
In the siddur these ‘aliyot are not listed or printed, only a note that says “see there” i.e. where they are printed for the festival day of Carpentras.
